title: The Suite runs its checks together, and a check can wait for its paths

statements.says: Every repo's Suite starts all its checks at once, after every readiness command has run one by one.
A red check does not stop the others; they all finish.
The Suite output keeps the order of the Suite file, not the order the checks ended in.
A check can name, with when, the paths that wake it, and then runs only when the ticket's own change touches one of those paths.
The ticket's change is the files that differ from the base its worktree was cut from, uncommitted work included.
Landing measures the change from the commit the ticket was rebased onto, so it is the ticket's own commits and nothing that came in on main.
A check without when always runs.
A change the loop cannot read runs every check.
A change that wakes no check runs every check, and the Suite output says why.
A check that did not run says so in the Suite output.
The comment that closes the ticket names what was not run beside what proved the work.
The preflight tests become a check of their own, woken by the script, its short command, its test, and the shared test support.
The architecture axis no longer runs the Suite at all, and runs only the checks the placement-checks file names, a decision an earlier record settled and owns.
Here the placement checks are the Architecture tests alone and the front end's lint.
Making the preflight tests cheaper while they stay in every Suite is still worth doing and is not ruled out.
The Suite had grown to take most of a ticket: across one spec the suite step took a median of 24 minutes.
Landing ran the Suite again whenever main had moved, and the architecture axis ran it once before its review and again after a fix.
Most of the Suite's time went to the 27 preflight tests, about 30 seconds each, proving a script that runs once when a repo sets the Plugin up.
Run together, the Suite takes as long as its slowest check, not the sum of them.
Letting every check finish means the fix Session reads every failure rather than the first.
Keeping the Suite file's order makes two runs of one Suite read the same.
Running a check that was not needed is the safe way to be wrong.
A Suite that ran nothing cannot pass, and a red one would stop every ticket that touches no watched path.
The API tests take six minutes and prove nothing about placement.
Making the preflight tests cheaper does not answer why a script that runs once is proved on every ticket.

The preflight check's wake list names the shared test support because a change to a file the preflight reads that is not on the list can break the preflight tests unseen until the next ticket that wakes them.
Running checks together only when the Suite file asks was rejected, because the loop is slow in every repo for the same reason, and a team whose checks collide can join them into one check.
Letting a red check stop the others was rejected, because a red Suite is rare and the fix Session gets one circuit, which it spends better knowing every failure.

A marker only this repo's tests know, turned off by the loop, was rejected, because the Machinery would carry a fact about one repo's tests, and when a check matters is part of what green means, which the Suite file already says.
Taking the change as everything that differs from origin/main now was rejected, because a change that came in on main already passed its own Suite and would wake checks the ticket never touched.
